achievement: Created ImageNet (14+ million labeled images); Time Person of the Year (2025); former Chief Scientist of AI/ML at Google Cloud; co-founder of AI4ALL; co-founder/CEO of World Labs; Princeton Woodrow Wilson Award; former Director of Stanford AI Lab (2013-2018)
title: Sequoia Professor of Computer Science; Co-Director, Stanford HAI
bio: Computer scientist known as 'The Godmother of AI,' best known for creating ImageNet, the massive visual database that catalyzed the deep learning revolution. She co-directs the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence and co-founded AI4ALL to increase diversity in AI.

name: Frances Pritchett
title: Professor of Modern Indic Languages
bio: Frances Pritchett is Professor of Modern Indic Languages in the Department of Middle Eastern, South Asian, and African Studies at Columbia University. Her research interests include classical Urdu ghazal, especially the work of Ghalib and Mir, and traditional narrative genres in Urdu and Hindi. Pritchett's translation of and commentary on Ghalib's ghazals can be found at her Columbia University website, along with links to her many other contributions to the understanding and appreciation of Urdu and Hindi literatures.
roundtables: Urdu Poetry: Ghalib and the Ghazal

name: Georges Didi-Huberman
institution: Ecole des Hautes Etudes en Sciences Sociales (EHESS), Paris
achievement: 2015 Adorno Prize; Corresponding Fellow of the British Academy (2017); curated major exhibitions at Centre Georges-Pompidou, Museo Reina Sofia, and Jeu de Paume; author of 'Images in Spite of All: Four Photographs from Auschwitz'
title: Maitre de Conferences, Centre d'Histoire et Theorie des Arts
bio: French philosopher and art historian whose research spans the visual arts, historiography of art, psychoanalysis, and philosophy. One of Europe's most wide-ranging interdisciplinary thinkers, he has published about thirty works on the history and theory of images from the Renaissance to contemporary art.
roundtables: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 1

name: Michael First
title: Professor of Clinical Psychiatry, Columbia University
bio: Michael B. First is a Professor of Clinical Psychiatry at Columbia University and a Research Psychiatrist at the New York State Psychiatric Institute. He is nationally and internationally recognized for his extensive work on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), having edited the text and criteria for DSM-IV, served as editor for DSM-IV-TR, and acted as editorial and coding consultant for DSM-5. He also serves as chief technical consultant on the World Health Organization's ICD-11 revision project.

name: Saeed Tavazoie
title: Professor of Biochemistry, Molecular Biophysics, and Systems Biology
bio: Tavazoie is a systems biologist who was professor in the Department of Molecular Biology and the Institute for Integrative Genomics at Princeton before joining the faculty at Columbia University in 2011. His research focuses on decoding the regulatory genome and revealing how networks of interacting genes implement complex phenotypes, with long-term goals centered on achieving a predictive understanding of biological behavior.
roundtables: Synthetic and Systems Biology: Reinventing the Code of Life

name: Stephen Dames
achievement: National Book Critics Circle Award finalist; PROSE Award in Literature (Association of American Publishers); Columbia Presidential Teaching Award (2005); Mark Van Doren Award for Teaching (2013); Great Teacher Award (2025); co-Editor in Chief of Public Books
title: Theodore Kahan Professor of Humanities; Paul Brooke Program Chair for Literature Humanities
bio: Literary scholar specializing in nineteenth-century British fiction who writes and teaches on the history and theory of the novel. His book 'The Chapter: A Segmented History from Antiquity to the Twenty-First Century' was a finalist for the National Book Critics Circle Award in Criticism.

name: Susan Wolfson
title: Professor of English
bio: Wolfson has taught at UC Berkeley and Rutgers University before joining Princeton. She specializes in British Romanticism literature, examining "enlightenment" quests for knowledge and philosophies of social freedom. Her teaching covers Shakespeare, Milton's Paradise Lost, nineteenth-century literature, and Modernism. She developed the Harvard Annotated Edition of Frankenstein (2012) with Ronald Levao and edited the annotated Northanger Abbey (2014). Recent publications include Reading John Keats (Cambridge UP 2015) and Romantic Interactions: Social Being and the Turns of Literary Form (Johns Hopkins UP 2010). She co-edits The Romantics and Their Contemporaries anthology (5th ed. 2012) with Peter Manning.

name: Elias Dakwar
achievement: NIH K23 award for ketamine-mindfulness research in cocaine use disorders; demonstrated that single-dose ketamine plus behavioral therapy promotes abstinence from cocaine; author of 'The Captive Imagination'; pioneer in psychedelic-assisted therapy for addiction
title: Associate Professor of Psychiatry
bio: Board-certified addiction and general psychiatrist who has spent over a decade researching novel treatments for substance use disorders. He is a principal investigator on several NIH-funded grants evaluating ketamine combined with behavioral therapies for treating cocaine, opioid, and alcohol use disorders.
roundtables: Coding and the New Human Phenotype: Is the Universe a Metaverse?

name: Arkady Plotnitsky
title: Distinguished Professor of Literature, Theory and Cultural Studies; Distinguished Professor of Philosophy and Literature
bio: Arkady Plotnitsky is a distinguished professor of Literature, Theory and Cultural Studies Program, and Philosophy and Literature program at Purdue University. He has published nine books, several edited or co-edited collections, and about two hundred articles on continental philosophy, Romantic and modernist literature, the philosophy of mathematics and physics, and the relationships among literature, philosophy, and science. His most recent book is Reality Without Realism: Matter, Thought, and Technology in Quantum Physics (Springer/Nature 2021). His next book Logos and Alogon: The Thinkable and The Unthinkable in Mathematics, from the Pythagoreans to the Moderns is forthcoming from Springer/Nature.

name: Bill Zavatsky
institution: Eugene Lang College of the New School (former); Trinity School in Manhattan (former); Morningside Heights Library (ongoing poetry workshop since 2013)
title: Poet
bio: Bill holds B.A. and M.F.A degrees from Columbia University and has taught across all educational levels since 1971. He authored three poetry collections and completed notable translations, including Andre Breton's Earthlight (with Zack Rogow), which won the PEN/Book-of-the-Month Translation Prize. His work has appeared in major anthologies and recordings by jazz pianists. The New York State Council on the Arts and National Endowment for the Arts both awarded him fellowships. He received MacDowell Colony fellowships in 2007-2008 and a Guggenheim Fellowship in Poetry in 2008.
roundtables: French Surrealism: A Revolution of the Mind

name: Christopher Johnson
achievement: Author of 'Hyperboles: The Rhetoric of Excess in Baroque Literature and Thought' (Harvard UP, 2010) and 'Memory, Metaphor, and Aby Warburg's Atlas of Images' (Cornell UP, 2012); translator of Francisco de Quevedo's Selected Poetry (Chicago UP, 2009); PhD in comparative literature from NYU
title: Professor of Spanish and Comparative Literature
bio: Scholar of early modern literature who has taught comparative literature at Harvard and early modern English literature at Northwestern. His work spans Spanish and English early modern literature, the rhetoric of excess in Baroque thought, and Aby Warburg's visual atlas project.
roundtables: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 2

name: Daphna Shohamy
title: Associate Professor of Psychology
bio: Dr. Shohamy's research combines brain imaging in healthy humans with studies of patients with brain disorders to understand how our expectations and experiences change the way memories are formed and the consequences for health and disease. She is the recipient of Young Investigator Awards from the Cognitive Neuroscience Society, the Society for Neuroeconomics, and the Association for Psychology Science.
roundtables: "Fake" Knowledge: Knowing and the Illusion of Knowing

name: Dennis Yi Tenen
title: Associate Professor, English & Comparative Literature
bio: Tenen is an associate professor at Columbia whose work examines the intersection of people, texts, and technologies. He previously served as a Microsoft engineer and fellow at the Berkman Center for Internet and Society, with code deployed across millions of computers globally. He earned his doctorate in Comparative Literature from Harvard under Elaine Scarry and William Todd's guidance. As co-founder of Columbia's Group for Experimental Methods in Humanistic Research and editor of the On Method series at Columbia University Press, he authored Plain Text: The Poetics of Computation (Stanford University Press, 2017). His scholarship appears in Modern Philology, New Literary History, Amodern, boundary2, and other journals, covering literary theory, media history, and computational narratology. His forthcoming work examines artificial intelligence's creative limitations.
roundtables: Coding and the New Human Phenotype: Are Natural Language Generators for Real?

name: Dhananjay Jagannathan
achievement: Author of 'Aristotle's Practical Epistemology' (Oxford University Press); PhD in Philosophy from University of Chicago (2017); teaches Literature Humanities in Columbia's Core Curriculum
title: Assistant Professor of Philosophy; Director of Graduate Studies, Classical Studies Program
bio: Philosopher specializing in ancient Greek and Roman philosophy, the history of ethics and political philosophy, and the intersection of philosophy and literature. His book 'Aristotle's Practical Epistemology' was published by Oxford University Press.

name: Dorothea von Mücke
title: Professor of Germanic Languages and Literatures
bio: Von Mucke holds a Ph.D. in Comparative Literature from Stanford University and has taught at Columbia since 1988, with visiting professorships in Berlin and Giessen. She specializes in eighteenth-century literature, Romantic literature, and literary theory. Her publications include three books: Virtue and the Veil of Illusion (1991), Body and Text in the Eighteenth Century (1994, co-edited), and The Seduction of the Occult and the Rise of the Fantastic Tale (2003). She co-edited The New History of German Literature (2004) and completed The Practices of the Enlightenment: Aesthetics, Authorship and Audiences, published by Columbia University Press in May 2015.

name: Edwin Turner
title: Professor of Astrophysical Sciences
bio: Turner holds an SB in Physics from MIT (1971) and a PhD in Astronomy from Caltech (1975). He joined Princeton's faculty in 1978 after brief appointments at the Institute for Advanced Study and Harvard. His research spans theoretical and observational astrophysics with over 250 publications covering binary galaxies, dark matter, gravitational lensing, exoplanets, astrobiology, and the origin of life. He directed Apache Point Observatory's 3.5-meter telescope for nine years and served on multiple boards including the Space Telescope Institute Council (three years as Chair). Recent interests include the Breakthrough Starshot Initiative, the YHouse project, artificial intelligence, and consciousness studies.

name: Elise Giuliano
achievement: Author of 'Constructing Grievance: Ethnic Nationalism in Russia's Republics' (Cornell UP, 2011); Director of MARS-REERS Program and Program on U.S.-Russia Relations; PhD in Political Science from University of Chicago; post-doctoral fellow at Harvard, Notre Dame, and Columbia
title: Lecturer in Political Science; Director of Graduate Studies, MA Program, Harriman Institute
bio: Political scientist specializing in the politics of ethnic identity, with particular focus on how ethnicity impacts popular attitudes and political mobilization. Her current research examines how the crisis in Ukraine has influenced political opinion among Ukrainian citizens in the country's eastern regions.

name: Elizabeth Barnes
achievement: Author of 'The Minority Body: A Theory of Disability' (Oxford UP, 2016) and 'Health Problems: Philosophical Puzzles About the Nature of Health' (2023); former editor-in-chief of Philosophy Compass; PhD from University of St Andrews
title: Professor of Philosophy
bio: Philosopher working in feminist philosophy, metaphysics, social philosophy, and ethics, known for her influential work on disability theory. In 'The Minority Body,' she argues that physical disability is not a defect but a form of human diversity, challenging dominant views in analytic philosophy.

name: Elizabeth Birkelund
achievement: Author of 'The Runaway Wife,' 'The Dressmaker,' and 'A Northern Light in Provence' (2024); Brown University (honors in Comparative Literature); Radcliffe Publishing Program; served on boards of National Humanities Center and The Center for Fiction
title: Novelist
bio: Novelist and former personal finance columnist for Cosmopolitan magazine. She has written for national magazines including Glamour, Self, and Working Woman, and is the author of several novels including 'The Runaway Wife,' 'The Dressmaker,' and 'A Northern Light in Provence.'

name: Harry L. Watson
title: Atlanta Distinguished Professor of Southern Culture
bio: Watson is a native of Greensboro, North Carolina, holding a bachelor's degree from Brown University and a doctorate from Northwestern. He joined UNC-CH's History Department in 1976. His scholarly focus encompasses American political history, the early American republic, and the antebellum South. He directed the UNC Center for the Study of the American South (1999-2012) and edited Southern Cultures journal (1993-2019). He has authored or edited eight books, including works on Andrew Jackson versus Henry Clay, Jacksonian politics, and a comprehensive narrative history of the American Republic to 1877.

name: Jared Weinstein
title: Professor, Mathematics & Statistics
bio: Jared Weinstein is a professor in the department of Mathematics and Statistics at Boston University, where he has worked since 2011. He specializes in number theory and its connections to other mathematical fields. A New York native, he earned his PhD from UC Berkeley in 2007.
roundtables: Permanence and Impermanence of Mathematical Concepts

name: Jeremy Veenstra-VanderWeele
title: Mortimer D. Sackler, M.D. Associate Professor of Psychiatry
bio: Dr. Veenstra-VanderWeele is a child and adolescent psychiatrist who uses molecular and translational neuroscience research tools in the pursuit of new treatments for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and related genetic syndromes. His training encompasses human molecular genetics at the University of Chicago and molecular neuroscience at Vanderbilt University. His research focuses on the serotonin, oxytocin and glutamate systems in genetic mouse models with abnormal social or repetitive behavior. He also maintains a clinical/translational program studying novel treatments for autism and Fragile X Syndrome. He joined Columbia University, the New York State Psychiatric Institute, and related affiliated institutions in 2014 to continue developing treatments for children with these conditions.

name: Mark Hansen
achievement: Eight patents; 60+ published papers; former Member of Technical Staff at Bell Laboratories; prior professor at UCLA; BS in Applied Math from UC Davis; MA and PhD in Statistics from UC Berkeley
title: Professor of Journalism; Director, David and Helen Gurley Brown Institute for Media Innovation
bio: Statistician and professor whose work lies at the intersection of data, art, and technology. His Computational Journalism course at Columbia contributed reporting for the New York Times' 'The Follower Factory,' which exposed the sale of fake Twitter followers and led to Twitter's 2018 purge of tens of millions of accounts.
roundtables: Coding and the New Human Phenotype: Coding, Fiction, Metafiction -- the Parcellation of What Isn't There

name: Michael Hecht
achievement: Created one of the first de novo designed proteins (Felix); discovered the first known de novo protein that catalyzes quantum dot synthesis; developed artificial proteins for insulin production with near 100% efficiency; pioneering work in synthetic biology and protein design
title: Professor of Chemistry
bio: Chemist and synthetic biologist whose research explores whether life can be sustained using molecular parts designed in the laboratory rather than evolved in nature. His lab designs artificial proteins from synthetic genes that are expressed in living cells, enabling the construction of artificial genomes with sequences never before seen in biology.
roundtables: Synthetic and Systems Biology: Reinventing the Code of Life

name: Nouchine Hadjikhani
achievement: Niclas Oberg Life Watch Award (2016); Leenaards Award (2010); pioneering fMRI research on migraine aura and autism neuroscience
title: Associate Professor of Radiology, Harvard Medical School; Professor in Experimental Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, University of Gothenburg
bio: Nouchine Hadjikhani is a neuroscientist whose research focuses on the pathophysiology of migraine and neurodevelopmental disorders, with particular emphasis on autism spectrum disorders. She discovered and characterized the brain area responsible for color vision using fMRI and demonstrated that the aura of migraine was a phenomenon similar to cortical spreading depression, in a groundbreaking paper cited more than 1,700 times. Her work disproving the theory that individuals with autism lack the brain area devoted to face identification has been highly influential in the field.

name: Patricia Dailey
achievement: Woodrow Wilson Postdoctoral Fellowship; translator of Giorgio Agamben's The Time That Remains (Stanford, 2005); co-founder of the University Seminar on Affect Studies
title: Associate Professor of English and Comparative Literature
bio: Patricia Dailey is a scholar of medieval literature and critical theory who joined the Columbia faculty in 2004. Her book Promised Bodies: Time, Language, and Corporeality in Medieval Women's Mystical Texts (Columbia University Press, 2013) examined the relation between gender, temporality, the body, and language in medieval mystical texts. She has translated works by Giorgio Agamben, Jean-Francois Lyotard, and Antonio Negri, and is a former Director of the Institute for Research on Women, Gender, and Sexuality.

name: Polly Young-Eisendrath
institution: Clinical and consulting practice in central Vermont
title: Psychologist, Jungian Psychoanalyst, Mindfulness Teacher, and Speaker
bio: Dr. Young-Eisendrath is a psychologist, speaker, Jungian analyst, and has published 15 books including The Self-Esteem Trap, The Resilient Spirit, Women and Desire, and The Present Heart: A Memoir of Love, Loss and Discovery. She came to psychology and Jungian training through the doorway of Buddhist practice, taking formal Zen vows in 1971. She views the dialogue between Buddhism and psychoanalysis as an emerging healing paradigm where ancient practices of awakening and liberation are meeting up with contemporary models of examining our minds. She is committed to building an interpersonally sustainable and ecologically sane world.

name: Spyros Papapetros
title: Associate Professor of Art and Architectural Theory and Historiography
bio: Spyros Papapetros holds an associate professorship at Princeton, where he also serves on executive committees for European Cultural Studies and Media and Modernity programs, plus holds a Behrman Faculty Fellowship. His scholarly interests encompass intersections among art, architecture, historiography, psychoanalysis, and aesthetics. He has received fellowships from the Getty Research Institute, Institute for Advanced Study, Canadian Center for Architecture, Barr Ferree Foundation, Townsend Center for the Humanities, and the Fulbright Program. During 2002-2003, he was an associate fellow at the Warburg Institute in London, researching unpublished Aby Warburg manuscripts. His published works include On the Animation of the Inorganic: Art, Architecture, and the Extension of Life (University of Chicago Press, 2012) and editorship of Space as Membrane by Siegfried Ebeling (Architectural Association Publications, 2010). His scholarship appears in October, Grey Room, Perspecta, RES, AA Files, Art Bulletin, Oxford Art Journal, and Journal for the Society of Architectural Historians. He co-edited Retracing the Expanded Field (MIT Press, 2014), examining architecture and visual arts intersections. Currently, he is developing World Ornament, examining architectural ornamentation and bodily adornment historiography from mid-19th to mid-20th century.
roundtables: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 2

name: W. Warner Burke
achievement: Fellow of the Academy of Management, Association for Psychological Science, and Society for Industrial and Organizational Psychology; Diplomate in organizational and business consulting psychology (American Board of Professional Psychology); co-developer of the Burke-Litwin Change Model
title: Edward Lee Thorndike Professor of Psychology and Education
bio: W. Warner Burke is a pioneering organizational psychologist who has been at Teachers College, Columbia University since 1979. He is co-developer of the widely studied Burke-Litwin Change Model and co-founder of the Eisenhower Leaders Development Program, jointly operated by Teachers College and the U.S. Military Academy at West Point. He has authored over 130 articles and book chapters and more than 15 books on organizational psychology, organization change, and leadership.

name: Alberto Bisin
achievement: Elected Fellow of the Econometric Society; Fellow of NBER and CEPR; co-editor of the Handbook of Financial Economics
title: Professor of Economics
bio: Alberto Bisin is an economist whose main contributions are in the fields of Social Economics, Financial Economics, and Behavioral Economics. He is an elected fellow of the Econometric Society and a fellow of the NBER, CEPR, and CESS at NYU. He is co-editor of the Handbook of Financial Economics and founding editor of noiseFromAmerika.org.

name: Alice Quinn
institution: Poetry Society of America; Columbia University (Adjunct Professor, Graduate School of the Arts)
title: Executive Director, Poetry Society of America
bio: Alice Quinn is the executive director of the Poetry Society of America and an adjunct professor at the Graduate School of the Arts at Columbia University. She was the Poetry Editor of The New Yorker for two decades and before that was an editor at Alfred A. Knopf. Ms. Quinn compiled a collection of Elizabeth Bishop's unpublished work in Edgar Allan Poe & The Juke-Box: Uncollected Poems, Drafts, and Fragments, which appeared in 2006. She is currently preparing a collection of Elizabeth Bishop's journals and notebooks.
roundtables: Elizabeth Bishop: A Conversation about Her Poetry

name: Joseph Salerno
achievement: Academic Vice President of the Mises Institute; editor of the Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics; Congressional testimony on monetary policy
title: Professor of Economics, Lubin School of Business, Pace University; Research Associate, NYU
bio: Joseph T. Salerno is an economist specializing in monetary theory and policy, international monetary reform, and Austrian economics. He is a research associate of the Foundations of the Market Economy in the economics department at New York University and has testified before Congress on inflation and fractional reserve banking. He serves as editor of the Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics and Academic Vice President of the Mises Institute.

name: Luis Cabral
achievement: Research Fellow of the Center for Economic Policy Research (CEPR); author of Introduction to Industrial Organization (MIT Press)
title: Paganelli-Bull Professor of Economics and International Business; Chair, Department of Economics, NYU Stern
bio: Luis Cabral is an economist specializing in industrial organization, with a focus on firm dynamics, innovation, platforms, and reputation in media and entertainment industries. He received his Ph.D. from Stanford University in 1989 under the supervision of Paul Milgrom and has previously taught at Yale, UC Berkeley, London Business School, and IESE Business School. He is the author of Introduction to Industrial Organization (MIT Press, 2000) and has published over 40 papers in specialized economics journals.
roundtables: The Changing Nature of Free Will

name: Miklos Toth
title: Professor of Pharmacology
bio: Toth is a neuroscientist whose laboratory investigates neuropsychiatric disease mechanisms using genetically modified mice to study anxiety, hyperactivity disorders, and behavioral abnormalities. His research examines genetic and environmental risk factors, including early adverse care, sedentary lifestyle, chronic societal stress, psychological trauma, and drug use. The lab explores how environmental stressors can trigger epigenetic changes linked to psychiatric conditions that persist across generations.

name: Nancy DiTomaso
achievement: C. Wright Mills Award from the Society for the Study of Social Problems (2013); Inequality, Poverty, and Mobility Section Distinguished Book Award from the American Sociological Association; Sage Award for Scholarly Achievement in Gender and Diversity (2016); past President of the Society for the Advancement of Socio-Economics
title: Distinguished Emerita Professor
bio: Nancy DiTomaso is a sociologist and management scholar whose research addresses diversity, culture, and inequality, as well as the management of knowledge-based organizations. Her 2013 book The American Non-Dilemma: Racial Inequality without Racism (Russell Sage Foundation) argues that America's racial divide is sustained more by whites' preferential treatment toward each other than by overt racial discrimination. She served as chair of the Department of Management and Global Business for twelve years and as Vice Dean of Faculty and Research.

name: Paul Linton
achievement: NOMIS Foundation Fellowship; Presidential Scholar in Society and Neuroscience at Columbia; author of The Perception and Cognition of Visual Space (Palgrave Macmillan, 2017)
title: NOMIS Foundation Fellow at the Italian Academy for Advanced Studies; Presidential Scholar in Society and Neuroscience
bio: Paul Linton is a neuroscientist and philosopher specializing in 3D vision whose research challenges fundamental assumptions about how we perceive depth and distance. His Ph.D. research at the Centre for Applied Vision Research, City, University of London demonstrated that the visual system is unable to triangulate distance using the two eyes. He is the author of The Perception and Cognition of Visual Space (Palgrave Macmillan, 2017) and lead editor of the Royal Society volume New Approaches to 3D Vision (2023).

name: Paula McDowell
achievement: John Ben Snow Foundation Prize (North American Conference on British Studies) for The Invention of the Oral
title: Professor of English
bio: Paula McDowell is a literary scholar specializing in eighteenth-century British literature and history, media history and theory, and the Marshall McLuhan archives. Her book The Invention of the Oral: Print Commerce and Fugitive Voices in Eighteenth-Century Britain (University of Chicago Press, 2017) won the John Ben Snow Foundation Prize from the North American Conference on British Studies. She is also the author of The Women of Grub Street: Press, Politics, and Gender in the London Literary Marketplace, 1678-1730 (Oxford, 1998).

name: Rebecca Seal
institution: Departments of Neurobiology and Otolaryngology, Center for Pain Research, University of Pittsburgh
title: Assistant Professor
bio: Dr. Seal is a tenure-track assistant professor in the Departments of Neurobiology and Otolaryngology and the Pittsburgh Center for Pain Research. Her research examines neurotransmitter transporters and their involvement in hearing, vision, motor function, and pain processing. As a postdoctoral scholar at UCSF, she discovered an important role for a specific neurotransmitter transporter in mechanical allodynia. Her laboratory currently investigates neural circuits underlying chronic pain to develop new therapeutic approaches. She has received numerous prestigious awards including recognitions from the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation, Rita Allen Foundation, Hearing Health Foundation, American Diabetes Association, and American Pain Society.

name: Selina Chen-Kiang
achievement: Researcher of the Year, Leukemia and Lymphoma Society; NCI Program Project Grant for Mechanism-Based Targeting of Mantle Cell Lymphoma ($9M+); Leukemia and Lymphoma Society Mantle Cell Lymphoma Research Initiative Award
title: Professor of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine
bio: Selina Chen-Kiang is an immunologist and cancer researcher whose work focuses on cell cycle control of B cell immunity and cancer, with particular emphasis on mantle cell lymphoma. She has received multiple grants from the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society over the past two decades, enabling her seminal work on therapies that target enzymes implicated in multiple cancers. She was awarded an NCI Program Project Grant from NIH/NCI in excess of $9 million for five years.

name: Theodore Shapiro
title: Professor Emeritus
bio: Theodore Shapiro is Professor Emeritus at the Weill-Cornell Medical College and a practicing psychoanalyst and adult, child and adolescent psychiatrist. He is a co-principle investigator on a study of psychodynamic psychotherapy for children and adolescents with anxiety disorders. He has more than 200 scholarly and research publications, is author of 7 books, and was Editor of the Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association from 1983-94. He has received the Rado, Brill, Hartmann, and Philip Wilson Awards and is a training/supervising analyst at New York Psychoanalytic Society and Institute.
roundtables: From Children's Sights to Our Insights: Ethiopian Children's Drawings, Stories and Inner Lives

name: Alma Steingart
title: Assistant Professor, History
bio: Alma Steingart researches the interplay between politics and mathematical rationalities. Her second book manuscript, Accountable Democracy: Mathematical Reasoning and Representative Democracy in America, 1920 to Now, examines how mathematical thought and computing technologies have impacted electoral politics in the United States in the twentieth century. She focuses on the census, apportionment, congressional redistricting, ranked voting, and election forecasts, investigating how changing computational practices have influenced definitions of "fair representation" of the American electorate. In Axiomatics: Mathematical Thought and High Modernism (2023, University of Chicago Press), she excavates the influence of axiomatic reasoning on mid-century American intellectual thought, spanning natural and social sciences, literary criticism, and modern design. Professor Steingart was a Junior Fellow of the Harvard Society of Fellows and a predoctoral research fellow at the Max Planck Institute for the History of Science in Berlin.
roundtables: Permanence and Impermanence of Mathematical Concepts

name: David Rosenthal
title: Professor of Philosophy and Coordinator of the Interdisciplinary Concentration in Cognitive Science
bio: David Rosenthal holds professorships in philosophy at the Graduate Center with courtesy appointments spanning linguistics and cognitive neuroscience. He coordinates the Graduate Center's Interdisciplinary Concentration in Cognitive Science. His scholarly work encompasses consciousness, mental perception, representational thought, emotions, and the self. His 2005 book, Consciousness and Mind, presents his theory that a psychological state is conscious if it is accompanied by a thought to the effect that one is in that state. Additional research addresses emotions, the mind-body problem, and thought-speech relations, with occasional forays into early modern and ancient philosophy plus methodological studies of philosophical history. He previously served as president of the Association for the Scientific Study of Consciousness and held visiting professorships at Nihon University (Tokyo) and Washington University (St. Louis), plus research fellowships at Universities of Bielefeld, Bremen, and Oxford. His credentials include a Ph.D. from Princeton and an A.B. from the University of Chicago.
roundtables: How Deep Do We Go? Behavior, Mind, and The 4-Billion-Year History of Life

name: Aaditya Rangan
title: Associate Professor, Mathematics
bio: Aaditya Rangan is an Associate Professor in the mathematics department at New York University. He received his B.A. from Dartmouth College, his Ph.D. from the University of California at Berkeley, and completed his postdoctoral work at NYU. His research has focused for many years on computational and theoretical models of sensory processing, particularly vision and olfaction.

name: Alan Richardson
title: Professor of English
bio: Alan Richardson holds degrees in English from Princeton University and Harvard University. Specializing in Romantic literature and culture, he has focused research on gender, childhood and education, race and colonialism, and scientific psychology. Over fifteen years, he has explored connections between literary studies and cognitive sciences. His published works include Literature, Education, and Romanticism: Reading as Social Practice (1994), British Romanticism and the Science of the Mind (2001), and The Neural Sublime: Cognitive Theories and Romantic Texts (2011). He has co-edited special issues and collections addressing Romanticism, slavery, and imperial culture, plus approximately fifty journal articles and book essays. His honors encompass a National Endowment for the Humanities Fellowship, Guggenheim Fellowship, Keats-Shelley Association Distinguished Scholar Award, American Conference on Romanticism book prize, and Alpha Sigma Nu National Jesuit Book Award. Current research examines literary and scientific conceptions of imagination from the Romantic era to the present.

name: Alex Abdo
achievement: Led landmark First Amendment litigation including challenge to Trump's blocking of Twitter critics; Yale College and Harvard Law School graduate
title: Litigation Director, Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University
bio: Alex Abdo is a First Amendment litigator who has been at the forefront of legal challenges involving government surveillance, free speech, and digital rights. At the Knight Institute, he has litigated cases challenging the government's prepublication review system, the constitutionality of government officials blocking critics on social media, and the secrecy of Office of Legal Counsel opinions. He previously spent eight years at the ACLU litigating cases relating to NSA surveillance, encryption, and post-9/11 abuse of detainees.

name: Andrea Gadberry
achievement: Author of Cartesian Poetics: The Art of Thinking (University of Chicago Press, 2020); coeditor of the Thinking Literature series
title: Associate Professor of Comparative Literature (joint appointment with Gallatin School of Individualized Study)
bio: Andrea Gadberry is a scholar of literature and philosophy in early modern and Enlightenment Europe, with additional interests in poetics, political theory, psychoanalysis, and critical theory. Her first book, Cartesian Poetics: The Art of Thinking (University of Chicago Press, 2020), defends the resultless enterprises of poetry and thinking by enlisting Rene Descartes as an unlikely ally. She is coeditor with Nan Z. Da of the Thinking Literature series.
roundtables: Touch as the Ur-Sense: From Presence to Poesy

name: Andreas Keller
title: Neuroscientist and Philosopher of Olfaction, Rockefeller University
bio: Andreas Keller is a Guest Investigator at Rockefeller University who studies human odor perception, conducting research at the intersection of cognitive neuroscience and philosophy with a focus on olfaction. He holds PhDs in both neuroscience from the University of Wurzburg and philosophy from the City University of New York. His landmark study in the Laboratory of Neurogenetics and Behavior demonstrated that humans can distinguish more than one trillion odor mixtures, and he is the author of Philosophy of Olfactory Perception.
roundtables: Discovering the What and the Wherefore: Scents and Sensibility

name: Anna Balas
achievement: Distinguished Life Fellow of the American Psychiatric Association; Training and Supervising Analyst at the New York Psychoanalytic Institute; member of the Association for Child Psychoanalysis
title: Clinical Associate Professor of Psychiatry
bio: Anna Balas is a board-certified psychiatrist, child psychiatrist, and psychoanalyst with a special interest in transcultural factors and creativity. She is a Training and Supervising Analyst at the New York Psychoanalytic Institute, where she teaches young child psychiatry and psychoanalysis students. Her teaching focuses on child development, transgenerational transmission of trauma, psychic trauma, and narcissism.

name: Apkar Apkarian
achievement: Pioneer in fMRI-based pain research; first to identify grey matter changes related to chronic back pain (2004); first to describe resting state network changes in chronic pain patients (2008); proposed chronic pain as emotional learning theory
title: Professor of Physiology, Anesthesiology, and Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation; Director, Center for Translational Pain Research
bio: Apkar Vania Apkarian is a neuroscientist and pioneer in the use of fMRI and magnetic resonance spectroscopy to study the neurochemistry of the brain, including the first demonstration of the brain's small-world network properties using fMRI. In 2008, he proposed the influential theory that chronic pain is a form of emotional learning, which transformed the study of reward learning within the pain research field. His research was pivotal in establishing neuroplasticity as a mechanism of chronic pain, first identifying grey matter changes related to chronic back pain in 2004.

name: Dmitry Rinberg
title: Professor, Department of Neuroscience & Physiology
bio: Dr. Rinberg earned his Ph.D. in Physics from the Weizmann Institute of Science before transitioning to neuroscience research. His work focuses on three main areas: deciphering the fundamental principles of neural coding, exploring olfactory information processing in the brain, and harnessing the olfactory system's remarkable sensitivity as a chemical detector. The lab has developed theoretical frameworks and technologies for brain communication. Beyond his academic role, he directs an NIH-funded consortium called "Cracking the Olfactory Code" involving seven research institutions, and founded Canaery, a startup developing odor digitization through Brain-Machine Interface technology.
roundtables: Discovering the What and the Wherefore: Scents and Sensibility

name: Eric R. Marcus
achievement: Columbia University President's Teaching Award; Roeske Teaching Award (American Psychiatric Association); Shabshin Teaching Award (American Psychoanalytic Association); Distinguished Life Fellow of the American Psychiatric Association; Fellow of the New York Academy of Medicine
title: Director, Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research; Professor of Clinical Psychiatry
bio: Eric R. Marcus is a psychiatrist and psychoanalyst who directs the Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research. His research involves symbolic alterations of reality in psychotic and near psychotic phenomena, and psychodynamic social science research using medical student dreams to study the development of medical empathy. He is a distinguished life fellow of the American Psychiatric Association and past president of the Association for Psychoanalytic Medicine.

name: Erica Robles-Anderson
title: Associate Professor of Media, Culture, & Communication
bio: Robles-Anderson holds an Associate Professor position at NYU and received the 2023-24 Leonore Annenberg and Wallis Annenberg Fellowship at Stanford. She serves as editor-in-chief of Public Culture. Her research examines how media technologies create space, particularly configurations that produce public or collective experiences through visibility structures. With training in experimental psychology and cultural history, she employs diverse methodologies to study media-space. Currently, she is authoring a book on 20th-century Protestant worship transformation into mediated "mega-churches" (Yale University Press contract). Previously, she was a Research Fellow in New Media and Architecture at the University of Umea's Department of Culture and Media and Humanities and Technology Laboratory. She holds a Ph.D. in Communication from Stanford University.

name: James Higham
achievement: Director of the Primate Reproductive Ecology and Evolution group; faculty member of the New York Consortium in Evolutionary Primatology
title: Professor of Anthropology
bio: James Higham is a biological anthropologist who studies sexual selection and communication in primates, exploring signaling behavior from genetic, neuroendocrine, behavioral, and morphological perspectives. He directs the Primate Reproductive Ecology and Evolution group, with ongoing fieldwork projects on communication systems in macaques, guenons, and baboons in Nigeria, Puerto Rico, and Indonesia. His research integrates game theoretic signaling models with computational modeling of primate perception.

name: Kathryn Hall
achievement: Coined the term 'placebome'; author of Placebos (MIT Press, 2022); Deputy Commissioner of Population Health and Health Equity, Boston Public Health Commission
title: Assistant Professor of Medicine (part-time), Harvard Medical School; Director of Placebo Genetics, Program in Placebo Studies, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center
bio: Kathryn T. Hall is a molecular biologist and leader in placebo research who coined the term 'placebome' to describe the genetic underpinnings of the placebo effect. She directs placebo genetics research in the Program in Placebo Studies at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and basic and translational research at the Osher Center for Integrative Medicine at Brigham and Women's Hospital. Her 2022 book Placebos (MIT Press) summarizes her research, which has been featured in The Atlantic, Science Magazine, The Economist, and The New York Times.
roundtables: Panacea or Poison: Placebos and Nocebos in Modern Medicine

name: Kristen Lindquist
achievement: Rising Star Award, Association for Psychological Science (2013); Fellow of the Society for Experimental Social Psychology; Fellow of the Association for Psychological Science
title: Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience (incoming Robert K. and Dale J. Weary Chair in Social Psychology, Ohio State University)
bio: Kristen Lindquist is a social psychologist and affective neuroscientist whose research demonstrates that emotions are not localized to single brain regions but rely on distributed neural networks, challenging the view that 'basic emotions' are universal. Her work on emotion words shows that speakers of different languages likely convey different meanings when discussing emotions like love, countering assumptions about emotional universality. She directed the Affective Science Lab at UNC Chapel Hill and is the incoming Weary Chair in Social Psychology at Ohio State University.
roundtables: How Deep Do We Go? Behavior, Mind, and The 4-Billion-Year History of Life

name: Larry Amsel
achievement: Co-director of Trauma Studies and Services Division at NYSPI following 9/11; organized first APA symposium on game theory and psychiatry (2003); Yale School of Medicine graduate with MPH from Columbia
title: Assistant Professor of Clinical Psychiatry
bio: Larry V. Amsel is an academic psychiatrist whose research spans the treatment of PTSD and trauma sequelae, applications of behavioral economics and game theory to psychiatry, and forensic psychiatry. Following 9/11, he co-directed the Trauma Studies and Services Division at the New York State Psychiatric Institute and has been extensively involved in treating victims and training clinicians in cutting-edge treatments for PTSD and complicated grief. In 2003, he organized the first American Psychiatric Association symposium on applications of game theory to psychiatry.

name: Laura Hirshbein
achievement: Robert Wood Johnson Foundation Investigator Award; dual MD (University of Michigan) and PhD in History of Medicine (Johns Hopkins); specialist in the history of psychiatry and diagnostic evolution
title: Professor of Psychiatry
bio: Laura Hirshbein is a psychiatrist and historian of medicine who holds both an MD from the University of Michigan and a PhD in the history of medicine from Johns Hopkins University. Her research focuses on the history of psychiatry, health policy, and diagnosis, with particular attention to transformations in child psychiatry and the evolution of DSM diagnoses for children. She is a Robert Wood Johnson Foundation Investigator Award recipient for her work on children's mental healthcare.

name: Linda Keen
achievement: Fellow of the American Mathematical Society (2012); Fellow of the Association for Women in Mathematics (inaugural class, 2017); President of AWM (1985-1986); Vice-President of AMS (1992-1995); known for the Collar lemma in hyperbolic geometry
title: Professor Emerita of Mathematics
bio: Linda Keen is a mathematician known for her work on Riemann surfaces, hyperbolic geometry, Kleinian groups, Fuchsian groups, and complex analysis. She earned her PhD from NYU's Courant Institute in 1964 under the direction of Lipman Bers and has been on the faculty of CUNY since 1965. She served as president of the Association for Women in Mathematics (1985-1986), vice-president of the American Mathematical Society (1992-1995), and is known in hyperbolic geometry for the Collar lemma.

name: Mahan Azadpour
achievement: Specialist in cochlear implant and auditory brainstem implant research; expertise spanning psychophysics, electrophysiology, and computational modeling of auditory perception
title: Research Associate Professor, Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery
bio: Mahan Azadpour is a neuroscientist and biomedical engineer who researches cochlear implant and auditory brainstem implant devices, among the most successful neural interface technologies. He began his academic career at Sharif University of Technology in Iran, earning a graduate degree in Electrical and Biomedical Engineering, then pursued his PhD in Cognitive Neuroscience at the International School for Advanced Studies in Italy. His research employs psychophysics, electrophysiology, and computational modeling to improve assistive technologies for hearing-impaired individuals.
roundtables: Striking a Chord: Hearing and Space

name: Paul Zelinsky
institution: Board of the Society of Children's Book Writers and Illustrators; Co-chair of the Children's and Young Adult Committee of PEN American Center
title: Children's Book Illustrator and Author
bio: Paul O. Zelinsky is a children's book illustrator and writer whose books have won wide acclaim and many awards, including the Caldecott Medal for his retelling of Rapunzel, and three Caldecott Honors. He earned an M.F.A. in Painting from Tyler School of Art and a B.A. from Yale College, where he studied under Maurice Sendak. His work spans multiple styles and genres, from Renaissance-inspired oil paintings in fairy tales to cartoonish illustrations. His books communicate effectively with children across developmental levels, including those with learning disabilities or autism. He volunteers with organizations promoting children's literature and literacy.

name: Penelope Lewis
achievement: Author of 'The Secret World of Sleep'; TEDx speaker on sleep engineering; research featured on BBC; funded by Wellcome Trust and UK research councils; contributor to New Scientist, Scientific American, and BBC Focus
title: Professor of Psychology
bio: Penelope Lewis is a neuroscientist and Professor of Psychology at Cardiff University, where she directs the Neuroscience and Psychology of Sleep (NAPS) lab. Her research investigates the role of sleep in strengthening and transforming memories, using methods such as targeted memory reactivation. She is the author of 'The Secret World of Sleep: The Surprising Science of the Mind at Rest,' which has been translated into Japanese and Chinese.

name: Richard Betts
achievement: Woodrow Wilson Award from the American Political Science Association for best book in political science; five prizes for his writings; served on the National Commission on Terrorism (Bremer Commission); Adjunct Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations
title: Leo A. Shifrin Professor Emeritus of War and Peace Studies
bio: Richard K. Betts is an American political scientist and international relations scholar specializing in U.S. national security, military strategy, and intelligence. He served as director of the Saltzman Institute of War and Peace Studies and the International Security Policy Program at Columbia's School of International and Public Affairs. He has consulted for the National Intelligence Council, the National Security Council, and the CIA.

name: Allison Avery
title: Vice President of Inclusion and Community, Dow Jones; Jungian Psychoanalyst
bio: Allison Avery is a diversity, equity, and inclusion executive and Jungian psychoanalytic candidate. She holds a Master of Arts in Applied Psychology from New York University and a professional certificate in HR Management from Cornell University's ILR School. She previously served as the first Director of Diversity and Inclusion at NYU School of Medicine and maintained a private psychoanalytic practice for over nine years while completing certification through the International Association of Analytical Psychology.

name: Ben Kafka
title: Associate Professor of Media, Culture, and Communication, NYU
bio: Ben Kafka is an Associate Professor of Media, Culture, and Communication at New York University, specializing in media history and theory. He holds a PhD in history from Stanford University and is the author of The Demon of Writing: Powers and Failures of Paperwork (2012). He is also a trained psychoanalyst affiliated with Columbia University's Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research, and has been a fellow at Princeton's Society of Fellows and the Institute for Advanced Study.

name: Bonnie Costello
title: William Fairfield Warren Distinguished Professor of English, Boston University
bio: Bonnie Costello is the William Fairfield Warren Distinguished Professor and Professor of English Emerita at Boston University, where she has taught since 1977. An internationally recognized literary critic and authority on modern American poetry, she has written extensively about Marianne Moore, Elizabeth Bishop, Wallace Stevens, and John Ashbery. She is a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and has received Guggenheim, Rockefeller, and NEH research fellowships.
roundtables: Elizabeth Bishop: A Conversation about Her Poetry

name: Dennis Overbye
title: Cosmic Affairs Correspondent
bio: Dennis Overbye covers science topics ranging from "the mating habits of black holes and zero-gravity fashion shows to science in the movies, the status of Pluto and the fate of the universe" for the New York Times. He authored two books: Lonely Hearts of the Cosmos (1991), a National Book Critics Circle award finalist, and Einstein in Love (2000). His Higgs boson reporting was a Pulitzer Prize finalist in 2014. He has received recognition from the National Academy of Sciences, AAAS, the American Institute for Physics, and the American Astronomical Society. Born in Seattle in 1944, Overbye earned a physics degree from MIT in 1966. He worked at Sky and Telescope and Discover magazines before joining the New York Times in 1998. He resides in New York City with his wife Nancy Wartik and daughter Mira.

name: Elizabeth Waters
title: Democracy and Knowledge Consultant
bio: Elizabeth Waters (Ph.D.) is a democracy and knowledge consultant. Her training in learning and memory neuroscience naturally led her to become an educator. Elizabeth works with students, teachers, and communities to explore the boundaries of our current knowledge and the practices that support this exploration.

name: Gabbrielle Johnson
achievement: Published 'The Structure of Bias' and other influential papers on implicit bias in computational systems; former Bersoff Faculty Fellow at NYU
title: Assistant Professor of Philosophy
bio: Gabbrielle M. Johnson is a philosopher specializing in the philosophy of psychology, cognitive science, and technology, with a focus on computational models in vision and social cognition. Her research extends theories of implicit bias beyond individual agents to biases in machine learning algorithms and structural systems of injustice. She earned her PhD from UCLA and was a Bersoff Faculty Fellow at NYU's Center for Mind, Brain, and Consciousness.

name: James Berger
title: Senior Lecturer in American Studies and English, Yale University
bio: James Berger is a Senior Lecturer in American Studies and English at Yale University, where he teaches courses on apocalyptic literature, utopias and dystopias, and disability studies. He holds a PhD from the University of Virginia and is the author of After the End: Representations of Post-Apocalypse (1999) and The Disarticulate: Language, Disability, and the Narratives of Modernity (2014). He is also a published poet and plays in multiple jazz bands.

name: James Judd
achievement: Music Director Emeritus of the NZSO; former Music Director of the Israel Symphony Orchestra Rishon LeZion; Artistic Director of the Daejeon Philharmonic Orchestra; recorded Brahms symphonies with the Royal Philharmonic for Decca
title: Conductor and Music Director Emeritus
bio: James Judd is a British conductor who came to international attention as Assistant Conductor of the Cleveland Orchestra under Lorin Maazel and was appointed Associate Music Director of the European Community Youth Orchestra by Claudio Abbado. He served as the last full-time Music Director of the Florida Philharmonic (1987-2001) and as the first Music Director of the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra (1999-2007), where he now holds the title Music Director Emeritus.

name: Jill Gordon
achievement: Author of 'Turning Toward Philosophy: Literary Device and Dramatic Structure in Plato's Dialogues'; cofounder and first co-director of the Ancient Philosophy Society; PhD from University of Texas at Austin
title: NEH/Class of 1940 Distinguished Professor of the Humanities, Emerita; Professor of Philosophy, Emerita
bio: Jill Gordon is a philosopher specializing in ancient Greek philosophy (primarily Plato) and social philosophy (race, economic inequality, feminist philosophy). She served as Vice President for Academic Affairs and Dean of Faculty at Pitzer College, and as Coordinator of Women's Studies for the Claremont Colleges. She cofounded the Ancient Philosophy Society and Colby's Simone de Beauvoir Society.
roundtables: Striking a Chord: Hearing and Space

name: Katalin Balog
achievement: Her paper 'Conceivability, Possibility, and the Mind-Body Problem' (The Philosophical Review, 1999) was selected by The Philosopher's Annual as one of the ten best philosophy articles of 2000; former faculty at Cornell and Yale
title: Professor of Philosophy
bio: Katalin Balog is a philosopher whose research centers on consciousness, the self, subjectivity, and the mind-body problem. Born in Budapest, she came to the United States in 1989 and earned her PhD at Rutgers-New Brunswick. Before joining Rutgers-Newark, she taught at Cornell and Yale for over a decade.
roundtables: Come Out Wherever You Are: In Search of Consciousness

name: Patricia Bauer
title: Asa Griggs Candler Professor of Psychology, Emory University
bio: Patricia J. Bauer is the Asa Griggs Candler Professor of Psychology at Emory University, widely recognized for her research on the early development of memory in children, with a focus on autobiographical memory. She earned her PhD in Experimental Developmental Psychology from Miami University and previously held faculty positions at the University of Minnesota and Duke University. She received the APA Distinguished Scientific Award for an Early Career Contribution to Psychology in 1993.

name: Sam McDougle
achievement: 2026 Cognitive Neuroscience Society Young Investigator Award; PhD from Princeton University; postdoctoral fellowship at UC Berkeley
title: Assistant Professor of Psychology
bio: Samuel D. McDougle is a cognitive neuroscientist who runs the Action, Computation, and Thinking (ACT) lab at Yale, investigating human learning, memory, and the interface between high-level cognition and motor behavior. His research uses psychophysical, computational, and neurophysiological techniques to study how motor skill learning involves an interaction between executive functions and low-level processes.

name: Sandra Shapshay
title: Associate Professor of Philosophy
bio: Shapshay earned her B.A. in Intellectual History from the University of Pennsylvania (1992) and her Ph.D. in Philosophy from Columbia University (2001). Her scholarly interests focus on 19th century German philosophy, especially Kant and Schopenhauer, as well as contemporary aesthetics and ethics. She has published extensively on Schopenhauer's theories of sublime experience and tragedy, including work on environmental aesthetics. Currently, she is developing a book titled Degrees of Inherent Value: Schopenhauer's Ethical Thought, which presents a hybrid Kantian-Moral Sense theory of ethics that promises to interject a novel, less-anthropocentric option into the ethical-theoretical landscape. She has received fellowships from the Deutscher Akademischer Austauschdienst (DAAD) and won the John Eliot Outstanding Teacher Award and a Trustees Teaching Award.

name: Vittorio Gallese
title: Professor of Psychobiology and Cognitive Neuroscience, University of Parma
bio: Vittorio Gallese is a Full Professor of Physiology at the University of Parma and a leading figure in the discovery of mirror neurons, which he first observed in macaque monkeys in 1991 alongside Giacomo Rizzolatti. His research on mirror neurons and embodied simulation theory has profoundly influenced understanding of social cognition, empathy, and action understanding. He received the 2007 Grawemeyer Award for Psychology and holds positions at the University of London and Columbia University.
roundtables: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 1

name: Andrew Guess
achievement: Published in Nature Human Behaviour and Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences; research on misinformation funded by major grants; affiliated with Princeton's Center for Information Technology Policy
title: Associate Professor of Politics and Public Affairs
bio: Andrew M. Guess is a political scientist who studies how people choose, process, spread, and respond to political information, using experimental methods, large datasets, and machine learning. His research investigates online polarization, the consumption and spread of misinformation, and the effectiveness of media literacy interventions.
roundtables: Coding and the Human Phenotype: Manipulated Perception? Fakery, Authenticity, and the Birth of NFTs

name: Anis Dizdarevic
achievement: Castle Connolly America's Top Doctor in Pain Medicine; Harvard Medical School fellowship; lectured at numerous national and international conferences in anesthesiology and pain medicine
title: Associate Professor of Anesthesiology; Director of Regional and Orthopedic Anesthesia
bio: Anis Dizdarevic is a physician-researcher specializing in anesthesiology and pain medicine, with particular expertise in perioperative pain management, ultrasound-guided interventions, and multimodal analgesia. He is fellowship-trained at Harvard Medical School and is actively involved in clinical care, research, and medical education.

name: Carol Mandel
achievement: 2011 Hugh C. Atkinson Memorial Award from the American Library Association; former President of the Association of Research Libraries; Vice Chair of the Board of the Council on Library and Information Resources (CLIR)
title: Dean Emerita of NYU Libraries; Distinguished Presidential Fellow at the Council on Library and Information Resources
bio: Carol A. Mandel served as Dean of New York University Libraries from 1999 to 2018, overseeing libraries across NYU's New York, Abu Dhabi, and Shanghai campuses, as well as Campus Media Services and NYU Press. Previously, she was Deputy University Librarian at Columbia University. She has served on the boards of the Association of Research Libraries, the Digital Library Federation, HathiTrust, and ITHAKA Harbors.
roundtables: The Library as Reality and Metaphor

name: Christine Vitrano
title: Associate Professor of Philosophy
bio: Christine Vitrano is the author of The Nature and Value of Happiness. She co-authored Happiness and Goodness: Philosophical Reflections on Living Well with Steven M. Cahn and co-edited Happiness: Classic and Contemporary Readings in Philosophy with him as well.

name: Daniel Goroff
institution: Alfred P. Sloan Foundation / Harvey Mudd College
achievement: 2020 Links Lecture Award from the American Statistical Association; Phi Beta Kappa Award for educational excellence at Harvard; PhD in Mathematics from Princeton; M.Phil. in Economics from Cambridge University
title: Vice President and Program Director, Alfred P. Sloan Foundation; Professor Emeritus of Mathematics and Economics
bio: Daniel L. Goroff is a mathematician and economist who serves as Vice President and Program Director at the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, where he oversees grants supporting breakthroughs in science, technology, and economics. He previously spent twenty years at Harvard University and served as Dean of the Faculty and Vice President for Academic Affairs at Harvey Mudd College.
roundtables: The Library as Reality and Metaphor

name: E. James Lieberman
achievement: Author of 'Acts of Will: The Life and Work of Otto Rank' (translated into German and French); editor of 'The Letters of Sigmund Freud and Otto Rank'; former Chief at NIMH Center for Child and Family Mental Health
title: Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Emeritus
bio: E. James Lieberman is a psychiatrist who practiced psychotherapy in Washington, D.C. for four decades after serving as Chief of the Center for Child and Family Mental Health at NIMH in the 1960s. He is a leading scholar on Otto Rank, having authored 'Acts of Will: The Life and Work of Otto Rank' and edited 'The Letters of Sigmund Freud and Otto Rank: Inside Psychoanalysis.'
roundtables: Male-Male Competition: Globalization, War, and Violence

name: Elizabeth Alter
achievement: Research Associate at the American Museum of Natural History; PhD from Stanford University; specialist in environmental DNA for marine biodiversity assessment and conservation genetics
title: Professor of Biology
bio: S. Elizabeth Alter is an evolutionary geneticist whose research uses genomic information to understand how biodiversity is created and maintained, particularly in aquatic species facing climate change and human impacts. She is a Research Associate at the American Museum of Natural History and specializes in population genomics, environmental DNA, and ancient DNA studies in threatened species.

name: Emma Levine
achievement: Named professorship (Charles M. Harper Chair); published in PNAS, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, and Psychological Science; BA and BS from University of Pennsylvania; PhD from Wharton School
title: Charles M. Harper Professor of Behavioral Science
bio: Emma E. Levine is a behavioral scientist whose research examines the psychology of altruism, trust, and ethical dilemmas, with a focus on how individuals navigate the tension between honesty and benevolence. Her work has been published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Psychological Science, and the Academy of Management Journal.

name: Ernesto Reuben
title: Assistant Professor of Management
bio: Ernesto Reuben is an Assistant Professor at Columbia Business School whose research focuses on behavioral and public economics. His work examines the role played by social norms and particular psychological traits on activities that are economically relevant for public policy and business strategy. His primary interests include prosocial and antisocial behavior microfoundations, group heterogeneity effects on norm enforcement, and competition's role in team performance. Recent work addresses reciprocity between interest groups and politicians, present-biased preferences and procrastination, and how implicit associations influence expectations and discrimination. He has taught public economics, microeconomics, experimental economics, statistics, and strategy at Princeton University, University of Amsterdam, Norwegian School of Management, and Kellogg School of Management.

name: John McGann
title: Professor of Behavioral and Systems Neuroscience and Director of the Center for Cognitive Science, Rutgers University
bio: John McGann is a Professor of Psychology and Director of the Center for Cognitive Science at Rutgers University, where he directs the Laboratory on the Neural Basis of Sensory Cognition. His research uses the olfactory system to study how learning changes sensory processing in the brain, and his landmark 2017 paper in Science debunked the long-held myth that humans have a poor sense of smell. He holds a PhD in Neuroscience from Yale University.
roundtables: Discovering the What and the Wherefore: Scents and Sensibility

name: Karen B. Stern
title: Professor of History
bio: Karen B. Stern is Professor of History at Brooklyn College of the City University of New York. Her research is deeply interdisciplinary. She studied Classics with honors at Dartmouth College, earned her M.A. and Ph.D. in Religious Studies from Brown University, and has excavated and conducted field research in different areas of the Mediterranean, including Jordan, Greece, Tunisia, Morocco, and Israel. Several grants, fellowships, and residencies from the National Endowment for the Humanities, Council of American Overseas Research Centers and the Getty Villa have supported her research, which deploys methods from fields of archaeology, anthropology, epigraphy, history, and religion to investigate the daily lives and material culture of Jews and Christians in antiquity. She is author of Inscribing Devotion and Death: Archaeological Evidence for Jewish Populations of North Africa (Brill 2007); and Writing on the Wall: Graffiti and the Forgotten Jews of Antiquity (2018; paperback ed. 2020), winner of a 2020 Jordan Schnitzer Book Award through the Association for Jewish Studies. She is preparing a museum exhibition on holy graffiti.
roundtables: Coding and the New Phenotype: In Search for Lost Time

name: Michael Novacek
title: Curator & Professor of Paleontology; Senior Advisor to the Museum's President
bio: Dr. Novacek earned his doctorate from UC Berkeley and specializes in evolutionary patterns and organism relationships across fossil records and DNA sequences. He has led paleontological expeditions across multiple continents including the Rocky Mountains, Andes, Saharan Africa, and Gobi Desert. He authored over 200 publications in peer-reviewed journals and popular media outlets. His notable books include Dinosaurs of the Flaming Cliffs (1996), Time Traveler (2002) -- both New York Times Notable Books -- and Terra: Our 100-Million-Year-Old Ecosystem (2007). He holds fellowships in the American Association for the Advancement of Science and American Academy of Arts and Sciences, plus honors including the 2003 Roy Chapman Andrews Distinguished Explorer's Award and 2005 Lowell Thomas Award.
roundtables: Coding and the New Phenotype: In Search for Lost Time

name: Paul Breslin
achievement: Three Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation Awards; American Psychological Association Distinguished Scientific Award for Early Career Contributions; President of the Association for Chemoreception Sciences; Distinguished Fellow in the National Academies of Practice
title: Distinguished Professor of Nutritional Sciences
bio: Paul Breslin is a geneticist, biologist, and taste perception researcher whose work focuses on taste discrimination, enhancement, suppression, and the genetic basis of oral perception and its impact on nutrient intake. He co-discovered that oleocanthal, a compound in extra-virgin olive oil, kills cancer cells without harming healthy cells. He holds dual appointments at Rutgers and the Monell Chemical Senses Center.

name: Richard Cohen
title: Author and Former Publishing Director
bio: Richard Cohen is a British author, editor, and former Olympic fencer who represented Great Britain at three Olympic Games and was a five-time British sabre champion. He served as publishing director of Hutchinson and Hodder & Stoughton, editing authors including John le Carre and Kingsley Amis. He is the author of By the Sword: A History of Gladiators, Musketeers, Samurai, Swashbucklers, and Olympic Champions, Chasing the Sun, and Making History: The Storytellers Who Shaped the Past.

name: Susan Seymour
achievement: 2004 Stirling Prize from the Society for Psychological Anthropology; author of 'Women, Family, and Child Care in India' and 'Cora Du Bois: Anthropologist, Diplomat, Agent'; PhD from Harvard University
title: Professor Emerita of Anthropology
bio: Susan Seymour is a cultural anthropologist whose research has focused on changing family and gender systems in India through a multi-decade longitudinal study in Bhubaneswar. She served as Vice President for Academic Affairs and Dean of Faculty at Pitzer College and as Coordinator of Women's Studies for the Claremont Colleges. Her most recent book is 'Cora Du Bois: Anthropologist, Diplomat, Agent' (2015).

name: Takis Pappas
title: Author & Researcher
bio: Takis S Pappas holds a PhD from Yale and is a Greek author and researcher currently affiliated with the University of Helsinki. He formerly served as a comparative politics professor at the University of Thessaloniki and has held academic positions at multiple institutions including Strasbourg, Oslo, Freiburg, Luxembourg, Central European University in Budapest, European University Institute in Florence, Yale, and Princeton. His published works include Making Party Democracy in Greece (Macmillan 1999), The Charismatic Party: PASOK, Papandreou, Power (2009), Populism and Crisis Politics in Greece (Palgrave 2014), On the Tightrope: National Crises and Brinkmanship in Greece (2017), Populism and Liberal Democracy: A Comparative and Theoretical Analysis (Oxford University Press 2019), and co-edited European Populism in the Shadow of the Great Recession (ECPR Press 2015). He is currently developing a book examining challengers of European liberal democracy, contributes as a columnist to Kathimerini newspaper, serves as a TED-Ed educator on populism, and maintains a blog on populism and democracy. He divides his time between Brussels and Athens.

name: Tom Carew
achievement: Former President of the Society for Neuroscience; Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science; NIMH MERIT Award; Yale's Dylan Hixon Prize for Excellence in Teaching; collaborated with Eric Kandel on foundational memory research
title: Professor of Neural Science; Former Dean of the Faculty of Arts and Science
bio: Thomas J. Carew is a neuroscientist whose research centers on the behavioral, cellular, and molecular analysis of learning and memory. In collaboration with Nobel laureate Eric Kandel, he provided the first evidence for long-term memory and associative learning in the sea slug Aplysia californica. He served as Dean of the Faculty of Arts and Science at NYU from 2011 to 2018.

name: Mark Polizzotti
title: Author & Translator; Director of the Publications Program, The Metropolitan Museum of Art
bio: Mark Polizzotti's books include Revolution of the Mind: The Life of Andre Breton, Highway 61 Revisited, Sympathy for the Traitor: A Translation Manifesto, Why Surrealism Matters, and Jump Cuts: Essays on Surrealism, Film, Music, Culture, and Other Utopian Topics. His writings have appeared in Apollo, Bookforum, The Brooklyn Rail, The Nation, The New Republic, The New York Times, The Paris Review, The Wall Street Journal, and elsewhere. His translations of works by Andre Breton, Marguerite Duras, Gustave Flaubert, Patrick Modiano, Scholastique Mukasonga, and Arthur Rimbaud, among others, have won or been shortlisted for the National Book Award, the Oxford-Weidenfeld Translation Prize, the Scott Moncrieff Prize, the International Booker Prize, the English PEN Award, the NBCC/Gregg Barrios Prize, and the French-American Foundation Translation Prize. A member of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences, a Chevalier of the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, and the recipient of an American Academy of Arts and Letters Award for Literature, he lives in New York, where he directs the publications program at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
roundtables: French Surrealism: A Revolution of the Mind

name: Yi-Yuan Tang
title: Professor of Psychological Sciences, Presidential Endowed Chair in Neuroscience; Founding Director of Texas Tech Neuroimaging Institute
bio: Dr. Tang holds prestigious fellowships with the Association for Psychological Sciences and American Psychological Association. His research spans cognitive, social, and affective neuroscience, examining brain mechanisms underlying attention, mathematics, language, decision-making, and creativity. He developed Integrative Body-Mind Training (IBMT), a mindfulness-based intervention studied since the 1990s through randomized clinical trials. Research demonstrates IBMT reduces stress, enhances attention and cognitive performance, improves emotion regulation and immune function, and promotes neuroplasticity across the lifespan. Applications include addiction, mood disorders, ADHD, mild cognitive impairment, and traumatic brain injury. He has authored 6 books and over 280 peer-reviewed articles published in prestigious venues including Nature, Science, and PNAS, with findings covered by TIME, New York Times, BBC, and NPR.

name: Alan Hirshfeld
achievement: Hirshfeld-Dowd Observatory at UMass Dartmouth named in his honor; Vice-Chair of the American Astronomical Society's Historical Astronomy Division; 'Starlight Detectives' finalist for the 2016 Julia Ward Howe writing award; Princeton BS, Yale PhD
title: Professor of Physics (Emeritus)
bio: Alan Hirshfeld is a physicist, astronomer, and science historian who has authored several acclaimed books on the history of scientific discovery, including 'Parallax: The Race to Measure the Cosmos,' 'The Electric Life of Michael Faraday,' 'Eureka Man: The Life and Legacy of Archimedes,' and 'Starlight Detectives.' He is an Associate of the Harvard College Observatory and a regular science-book reviewer for the Wall Street Journal.

name: Albert A. Johnstone
achievement: Author of 'Rationalized Epistemology: Taking Solipsism Seriously'; published 'The Deep Bodily Roots of Emotion' in Husserl Studies and 'The Basic Self and Its Doubles' in Journal of Consciousness Studies; PhD from University of Waterloo
title: Courtesy Professor of Philosophy
bio: Albert A. Johnstone is a philosopher working in the Husserlian phenomenological tradition, investigating subjective experience, embodiment, and consciousness. His research spans epistemology, somatology, phenomenology, and logic. His current project is 'The Pan-cultural Human: A First-Person Account.'

name: Avner Ash
achievement: Fellow of the American Mathematical Society (2012); PhD from Harvard under David Mumford; co-author of three popular mathematics books published by Princeton University Press
title: Professor of Mathematics
bio: Avner Ash is a mathematician whose research lies at the intersection of number theory, topology, group theory, and Galois theory. He has co-authored several popular mathematics books with Robert Gross, including 'Fearless Symmetry: Exposing the Hidden Patterns of Numbers,' 'Elliptic Tales: Curves, Counting, and Number Theory,' and 'Summing It Up: From One Plus One to Modern Number Theory,' all published by Princeton University Press.
roundtables: The Beauty and Unity of Mathematics

name: Bella Brodzki
achievement: National Endowment for the Humanities fellowships; Lucius Littauer Award; Hewlett-Mellon grants; BA from Sarah Lawrence College, MA from Hebrew University of Jerusalem, PhD from Brown University
title: Professor of Comparative Literature
bio: Bella Brodzki is a comparative literature scholar whose work spans world literature, translation studies, autobiography, literary and cultural theory, gender studies, and postcolonial studies. She is the author of 'Can These Bones Live?: Translation, Survival, and Cultural Memory' and co-editor of 'Life/Lines: Theorizing Women's Autobiography.' Her essays have appeared in PMLA, MLN, and Yale French Studies.

name: Cheryl Corcoran
achievement: Named Exemplary Psychiatrist by the National Alliance on Mental Illness; speech-as-predictor study ranked 2nd in Mount Sinai's Ten Medical and Scientific Breakthroughs of 2021; MD from Harvard Medical School; h-index of 36 with 120+ publications
title: Professor of Psychiatry and Program Leader in Psychosis Risk
bio: Cheryl Corcoran is a psychiatrist and researcher specializing in psychosis risk and schizophrenia. Her work uses MRI, EEG, and automated natural language processing to study disturbances in sensory processing, language, and social cognition across stages of schizophrenia. Her study on speech changes as predictors of schizophrenia risk was listed among the top ten medical and scientific breakthroughs of 2021 at Mount Sinai.

name: Christopher Mason
achievement: Principal Investigator for NASA Twins Study; Chair of NASA GeneLab steering committee (2018-2022); NIH Transformative R01 Award; NASA Group Achievement Award; Pershing Square Sohn Cancer Research Alliance Young Investigator Award; co-founded four biotech startups
title: WorldQuant Professor of Genomics and Computational Biomedicine; Director of the Initiative for Quantitative Prediction
bio: Christopher E. Mason is a genomicist and computational biologist whose lab identifies and characterizes essential genetic elements guiding the function of the human genome, with emphasis on elements orchestrating human brain development. He was a principal investigator for the NASA Twins Study and launched the PathoMap project to create the first genetic map of a city, leading to the International MetaSUB Consortium.
roundtables: Synthetic and Systems Biology: Reinventing the Code of Life

name: Craig Newschaffer
title: Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics; Founding Director, A.J. Drexel Autism Institute; Associate Dean for Research
